judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Inline link in the article paragraph: 'Critics say it would reduce public scrutiny and make it harder for communities and tribes to identify environmental harms...'. The href is a Sierra Club press release whose address reads 'sierra-club-baaja-remains-fundamentally-flawed-despite-manager-s-amendment' (the page itself returned 403 to my fetch). Read with its sentence, the link is a source for what critics say, and it leads to a critic's statement against the bill, so the text does match where it goes and its purpose can be determined from the link text with its sentence (2.4.4 passes). The live page has the same paragraph and link. The model had the sentence and the href and judged a mismatch wrongly.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Inline link 'projections from some organizations' in the sentence 'The advantage would likely tip toward renewable energy, according to projections from some organizations'. It leads to a C2ES press release, 'New Nationwide Analysis: Bipartisan Transmission Reforms Would Boost Clean Energy...', which presents modelling projections of the bill's effect on clean energy and gas (I opened it). The link text with its sentence describes that destination, so the claim is false and 2.4.4 passes. Live page unchanged for this link.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Inline link 'renewable energy projects' in 'Supporters say that would prevent costly delays, which can be particularly consequential for land-intensive renewable energy projects.' It leads to the Bipartisan Policy Center fact sheet 'The Environmental Case for Permitting Reform', which argues that land-intensive renewables are more likely to trigger long reviews (I opened it). The sentence makes the purpose clear (supporters' case about delays for renewables), and the destination matches it, so the claim is false and 2.4.4 passes. Live page unchanged.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: h4 'Looking Forward' inside a newsletter sign-up card, under the h4 'The climate news you need, right in your inbox. Always free.'; the card reads 'Fridays / Looking Forward / Climate news without the doom. Learn about climate solutions and how to be part of them. / Sign up' (screenshot checked). The heading is the newsletter's name and identifies what the card is about; in the newsletters section it describes its topic, which is what 2.4.6 asks. The live page has the same headings. The claim that it says nothing about the content under it is wrong.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Image link (tease art, tabindex=-1) to 'Is it OK to want a normal life during the climate crisis?', holding figure > img alt='Collage of person holding toddler's hands...'. The captured Chromium accessibility tree exposes the link with no name while the img has its alt name, so the claim is true of the capture. I reproduced it: in headless Edge a link wrapping figure > img alt gets an empty name (Chromium does not take name from contents through a figure), and on the live page, with the image loaded, this link still has an empty name, so the capture does not differ. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this is a 4.1.2 failure of the content: by the accessible name algorithm the figure is traversed and the name is the image's alt, axe-style checkers compute that name, and screen readers in browse mode read the image inside the link; others go by the name the browser exposes, which is empty in Chromium. So the label is uncertain. Separately, the alt describes the photo, not the story it links to (an R2 point for 1.1.1/2.4.4, not this claim).

judgments.label: false_positive

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: [visual context] '$15/mo' is one of three amount links ('$15/mo', '$25/mo', 'Other') in the donation appeal bar, linking to Grist's donation form with $15 monthly preselected. Its programmatic context is only its own list item ('$15/mo'); there is no title or aria-describedby, and the heading just before it in document order is a hidden cookie-dialog heading. The text that explains it, 'All Donations DOUBLED' and the 'Donate' link, sits in neighbouring elements, which the rubric does not count. '$15/mo' alone gives an amount and frequency but not that it is a donation, so the purpose cannot be determined from text plus context and the link fails 2.4.4; the claim names this. The live page has the same bar and markup, and the link is in the accessibility tree there.

Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this is a 4.1.2 failure of the content: by the accessible name algorithm the figure is traversed and the name is the image's alt, axe-style checkers compute that name, and screen readers in browse mode read the image inside the link; others go by the name the browser exposes, which is empty in Chromium. So the label is uncertain.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'Follow' in the site header navigation (next to 'Donate' and the menu button), href '#nav__item--link-follows-container', which opens a dropdown of 'Follow us on Facebook/Twitter/...' links and a newsletter form; that container is hidden until opened, so it adds no programmatic context. Even so, 'Follow' in a publication's header tells users the purpose: ways to follow Grist, which is what the link reveals. Its purpose can be determined from the link text, so 2.4.4 passes; the claim that the text does not tell where it goes is not accurate. Live page unchanged. (Whether a disclosure should be a button with aria-expanded is a 4.1.2 matter, not this one.)
